description: We are Vi@bilty42, we selected the challenge Lunar Landing Site Navigator.
summary:
Lumbra helps teams compare how a lunar landing site’s lighting and Earth visibility change with location and mission date. Select a named site or a point on the Moon, then explore Sun and Earth positions, terrain-aware visibility windows, the next sunset and Earthset, and idealized solar-flux estimates. A time-controlled 3D view shows the modeled sky from the site.

Explorer makes those conditions easy to inspect. Expert adds timelines, site rankings, mission-window searches, and a simplified check of when a modeled Deep Space Network station could see the site. It also lets teams compare south-pole candidates using regional iron oxide, titanium, or thorium abundance alongside lighting and Earth visibility.

Lumbra runs its calculations in the browser. Its Sun and Earth geometry has been checked against selected JPL Horizons cases; NASA lunar elevation data informs the regional terrain horizon. Results are for early comparison and planning, with terrain resolution, resource coverage, and communications limits stated in the app.
details:
What it does. Lumbra helps teams compare how a lunar landing site’s lighting and Earth visibility change with location and mission date. Users pick a named site or any point on the Moon and a UTC date range, and the app computes Sun and Earth elevation, terrain-aware visibility windows, their overlap, the next sunset and Earthset, and idealized solar-flux estimates.

Two modes. Explorer mode is visual and immediate: an interactive Moon globe, plain-language Sun and Earth verdicts, a time scrubber with play and loop, and a first-person sky view. Expert mode adds multi-day timelines (a week to a year), a best fixed-panel orientation, site ranking, mission-window search, a simplified check of when a modeled Deep Space Network station could see the site, and a regional abundance comparison (iron oxide, titanium, thorium) for south-pole candidates. Mast height changes the modeled horizon.

Intended impact. Faster early comparison of sites and dates when a mission slips, before moving to detailed analysis tools.

How it is built. TypeScript, React, Vite and Three.js, running entirely in the browser with no backend. Sun and Moon positions use astronomy-engine with the IAU 2015 lunar orientation and libration. The terrain horizon is computed from NASA lunar elevation data. The geometry was checked against selected JPL Horizons cases (DE441), within 0.02° in those cases.

What is creative. A time-first workflow, and a terrain-aware skyline instead of a flat-horizon assumption at the poles.

Limits. Earth visibility is not a link budget, and the DSN check is simplified geometry. Solar flux is idealized. The terrain grid (about 7.6 km) cannot resolve lander-scale ridges. Resource layers show regional abundance screening, not measured density at a landing point or evidence of extractable reserves. The 3D ground detail is illustrative.
dataRefs: NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit (LRO/LOLA elevation, LROC imagery)
Lunar Prospector reduced spectrometer products (NASA PDS)
projectRefs: IAU WGCCRE 2015 report on cartographic coordinates and rotational elements (lunar orientation model)
